Authors: Holmgren, A.J., Esdar, M., Husers, J., Coutinho-Almeida, J.
Primary_Determinants: Information governance; API mandate enforcement; exchange network structure
Key_Finding: Policy and governance structures are primary drivers of HIE interoperability adoption; information blocking rules reshaping vendor behaviour.
T_Construct_Examples: API compliance; FHIR mandate; information blocking prohibition
I_Construct_Examples: 21st Century Cures Act; interoperability mandates; regulatory incentives
Limitations: U.S. policy focus; limited to HIE context
Role_in_Paper: Institutional and policy anchor; cited in Methods, Results, Discussion
Notes: Covers 21st Century Cures Act enforcement; U.S.-centric

Authors: Eden, K.B., Totten, A.M., Kassakian, S.Z., Gorman, P.N., McDonagh, M.S., Devine, B., Pappas, M., Daeges, M., Woods, S., Hersh, W.R.
Primary_Determinants: Workflow integration; provider trust; financial barriers; policy incentives
Key_Finding: Adoption barriers span workflow, technical, financial, and policy layers; no single-domain explanation is sufficient.
U_Construct_Examples: Workflow disruption; provider trust; perceived usefulness
T_Construct_Examples: Technical integration failure; data quality concerns
Methodological_Strengths: Systematic methodology; broadest barrier taxonomy in evidence base
Limitations: 2016 — may not reflect FHIR/Cures Act era; HIE-specific
Role_in_Paper: Key systematic review; cited in Methods, Results (all domains), Discussion
Notes: All four UTIO domains represented; most cited source in paper

Primary_Determinants: Perceived usefulness; usability; training adequacy; organisational readiness
Key_Finding: Perceived usefulness, usability, training adequacy, and organisational readiness are key EHR adoption determinants.
U_Construct_Examples: Usability; perceived usefulness; training adequacy; user satisfaction
O_Construct_Examples: Resource capacity; small/rural org constraints; leadership
Methodological_Strengths: Large source pool; rigorous systematic methodology
Limitations: 2016 — pre-HITECH maturity; dated technology context; no explicit institutional domain
Role_in_Paper: Foundational EHR adoption determinant evidence; cited in Results (U, O domains)
Notes: Small and rural organisation resource constraints particularly prominent

Context: National-scale EHR programmes (AU, UK, NL, EE, IR)
Primary_Determinants: Leadership sponsorship; national strategy; stakeholder engagement; governance
Key_Finding: Successful national EHR programmes require coordinated leadership, governance, and stakeholder engagement across all implementation phases.
I_Construct_Examples: National digital health strategy; policy framework
Methodological_Strengths: Multi-country umbrella review; most comprehensive national-level review in evidence base
Limitations: Variable quality of included reviews; older data from some countries
Role_in_Paper: Umbrella-review anchor; cited in Background, Results (all domains), Discussion
Notes: Single most consistent success factor: senior leadership sponsorship

Authors: Aguirre, R.R., Suarez, O., Fuentes, M., Sanchez-Gonzalez, M.A.
Primary_Determinants: Alert fatigue; workflow disruption; unintended consequences; change management
Key_Finding: EHR benefits are moderated by workflow disruption, usability barriers, and unintended implementation consequences requiring structured change management.
U_Construct_Examples: Alert fatigue; workflow disruption; clinician satisfaction
O_Construct_Examples: Change management; go-live support; post-implementation monitoring
Limitations: Limited to EHR; excludes HIE/telehealth; no explicit institutional domain
Role_in_Paper: EHR post-implementation user readiness evidence; cited in Results (U domain)
Notes: Post-implementation focus; change management evidence strong

Authors: Torab-Miandoab, A., Samad-Soltani, T., Jodati, A., Rezaei-Hachesu, P.
Primary_Determinants: Semantic interoperability; syntactic standards; FHIR; HL7; terminology alignment
Key_Finding: Interoperability requires layered semantic, syntactic, and technical standards alignment; SNOMED CT, LOINC, FHIR R4 identified as essential components.
T_Construct_Examples: Semantic interoperability; syntactic interoperability; FHIR R4; HL7 v2; SNOMED CT; LOINC; CDA
Methodological_Strengths: Most technically rigorous source; standards-level detail; current (2023)
Limitations: Limited organisational/user domain coverage; technical focus only
Role_in_Paper: Technical interoperability anchor; cited in Results (T domain), Discussion
Notes: Semantic layer identified as highest-complexity interoperability challenge

Focus: eHealth adoption strategies from IT leader perspectives
Context: Senior IT leaders in healthcare organisations (N=10)
Primary_Determinants: Leadership support; training; vendor relations; regulatory compliance; organisational culture
Key_Finding: Six adoption themes from senior IT leader interviews support a multidimensional adoption model; leadership support is the single most-cited theme.
U_Construct_Examples: Training adequacy; user satisfaction; perceived usefulness
O_Construct_Examples: Leadership commitment; organisational culture; vendor governance
Methodological_Strengths: Qualitative depth; practitioner perspectives; all UTIO domains represented
Limitations: Small N=10; single qualitative case; limited generalisability
Role_in_Paper: Organisational execution qualitative evidence; cited in Results (U, O domains)
Notes: Rich organisational execution evidence from IT leader perspective

Authors: Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT
Focus: U.S. health IT adoption and interoperability progress
Primary_Determinants: FHIR API mandate; TEFCA; information blocking enforcement; HIE growth
Key_Finding: National EHR adoption progress depends on policy-driven interoperability mandates and exchange infrastructure maturity; FHIR APIs accelerating interoperability.
T_Construct_Examples: FHIR API compliance; ONC API certification; exchange infrastructure
I_Construct_Examples: HITECH; Cures Act; information blocking prohibition; TEFCA; QHINs
Methodological_Strengths: Most recent U.S. federal data (2025); authoritative source
Limitations: Descriptive; no causal inference; government framing and potential bias
Role_in_Paper: U.S. institutional context; cited in Results (I, T domains), Discussion
Notes: Covers 2024/2025 reporting cycle; TEFCA operational data included

Focus: NHS shared care record implementation and governance
Primary_Determinants: Information governance; data sharing agreements; clinical workflow integration
Key_Finding: Cross-organisational records require robust information governance frameworks and clinical workflow integration as primary enabling conditions.
I_Construct_Examples: National data opt-out; information governance frameworks; data sharing agreements
Role_in_Paper: NHS case primary source; cited in Results (I, O domains), Discussion
Case_Study: Yes — NHS Shared Care Records case
Notes: England NHS. National data opt-out and IG frameworks are central mechanisms

Focus: Estonian national eHealth system architecture and coverage
Primary_Determinants: X-Road data layer; legal mandate; provider participation; semantic standards
Key_Finding: Estonia's national system — operational since 2008 — achieves broad provider participation through legal mandate and X-Road secure data exchange architecture.
U_Construct_Examples: Patient portal (digilugu); clinician trust; citizen access
T_Construct_Examples: X-Road architecture; semantic interoperability; FHIR; national data standards
I_Construct_Examples: Legal mandate; EU EHR law; national digital strategy; GDPR compliance
Methodological_Strengths: Most recent Estonia data (2026); official source; highest adoption maturity case
Limitations: Grey literature; no peer review; national bias; O domain limited
Role_in_Paper: Estonia case primary source — highest maturity benchmark
Notes: Legal mandate produces near-universal provider upload obligation

Focus: Estonian EHR legal framework and national governance
Primary_Determinants: Mandatory upload obligations; national governance; data protection compliance
Key_Finding: Mandatory provider upload obligations and national governance underpin comprehensive EHR coverage; GDPR-compatible framework established.
T_Construct_Examples: Standardised data exchange; X-Road protocol requirements
I_Construct_Examples: EHR Law; mandatory participation; Personal Data Protection Act; legal mandate
Methodological_Strengths: Primary legal source; foundational for Estonia case
Limitations: Legal/policy only; no implementation evidence; 2016 (pre-FHIR mandate era)
Role_in_Paper: Estonia institutional framework anchor; cited in Results (I domain)
Notes: Legal framework basis for Estonia case; establishes institutional alignment baseline

Focus: VA EHR modernisation programme risks and outcomes
Primary_Determinants: User satisfaction deficits; vendor governance; configuration disputes; cost overruns
Key_Finding: Misalignment across user, technical, and organisational domains produces significant adoption risk despite strong institutional mandate.
U_Construct_Examples: Clinician satisfaction deficits; usability complaints; workflow mismatch
T_Construct_Examples: Configuration quality; system performance; interface reliability
O_Construct_Examples: Vendor governance; contract management; configuration disputes; cost overruns; schedule delays
Methodological_Strengths: Independent GAO audit; most recent VA data (2025); credible source
Limitations: Audit scope limited; no clinician-level qualitative data; DoD-specific framing
Role_in_Paper: VA/DoD case primary source — lowest adoption maturity benchmark
Notes: Oracle Health (Cerner) contract; persistent usability and vendor management failures

Context: U.S. Department of Defense Military Health System
Primary_Determinants: Issue management; user satisfaction; deployment acceleration; site variation
Key_Finding: User satisfaction deficits and systematic issue management failures undermine federal EHR adoption outcomes across MHS GENESIS deployment sites.
U_Construct_Examples: User satisfaction scores below targets; clinician resistance
T_Construct_Examples: Deployment quality; system configuration; interface performance
O_Construct_Examples: Issue management processes; reactive problem resolution; site-level variability
Methodological_Strengths: Independent GAO audit; federal scope; current (2024); 26 sites covered
Limitations: Audit scope; DoD-specific; limited to federal context
Role_in_Paper: VA/DoD case primary source — organisational execution gaps
Notes: MHS GENESIS. Issue tracking is reactive rather than proactive

Authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Primary_Determinants: Risk management framework; authorisation process; security governance
Key_Finding: Structured risk management frameworks support system trust, security governance, and organisational adoption readiness through formal authorisation.
I_Construct_Examples: Institutional security governance; risk authorisation; compliance baseline
O_Construct_Examples: Organisational risk management; system security governance
Methodological_Strengths: NIST authority; structured methodology; widely adopted
Limitations: Generic risk framework; not health-IT specific; no adoption determinant analysis
Role_in_Paper: Security governance baseline; cited in Background (institutional domain)

Authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Focus: Security and privacy controls for information systems
Primary_Determinants: Privacy controls; system integrity; access management; audit and accountability
Key_Finding: Security and privacy control baselines support governance compliance and system integrity — prerequisites for clinical system trust.
T_Construct_Examples: System integrity controls; privacy engineering; data protection
I_Construct_Examples: Regulatory compliance baseline; privacy law alignment
Methodological_Strengths: NIST authority; comprehensive control baseline; Rev 5 is current
Limitations: Security focus; limited direct user/workflow relevance
Role_in_Paper: Security and privacy governance baseline; cited in Background (institutional domain)
Notes: Rev 5. Provides institutional compliance baseline for health IT systems

Focus: PHI de-identification standards and safe harbour
Primary_Determinants: Safe Harbour method; expert determination; PHI de-identification standards
Key_Finding: Safe Harbour and expert determination standards enable lawful secondary use of de-identified health data, supporting research and interoperability.
I_Construct_Examples: HIPAA de-identification; privacy law compliance; Safe Harbour; expert determination
Limitations: Regulatory guidance only; no adoption evidence; U.S.-specific
Role_in_Paper: Privacy law compliance component of institutional domain
Notes: Enables data sharing without HIPAA PHI restrictions; supports interoperability

Primary_Determinants: System quality; information quality; use; user satisfaction; net benefits
Key_Finding: IS success depends on system quality and information quality leading to use, user satisfaction, and net benefits — foundational theoretical model for U and T domains.
U_Construct_Examples: Use; user satisfaction; perceived usefulness; net benefits
T_Construct_Examples: System quality; information quality; service quality
Methodological_Strengths: Highly cited; foundational IS theory; ten-year update with empirical validation
Limitations: 2003 — pre-EHR mandate era; theoretical only; not health-IT specific
Role_in_Paper: Theoretical foundation for U and T domain constructs; cited in Background
Notes: D&M IS Success Model. Underpins User Readiness and Technical Interoperability constructs
